_comment: Storyboard for the Grade 4 Computing unit lecture film, Lesson 12 Caesar and Pigpen. Rendered by tools/create-ehel-unit-lecture.js. See lecture-video/BRIEF.md. Every beat is one narration clip; art.at names the phrases a picture waits for, and the page refuses to load if a phrase is not in its beat's say. The chapters follow LESSON[lecture] in order (the Caesar cipher; the Pigpen cipher; the key; encryption today; the round trip and its four names). EVERY ENCIPHERED LETTER ON SCREEN IS THE LESSON'S OWN RULE: the strip, the word tiles, the twenty-five tries and the round trip all call ART.caesar, and every Pigpen glyph and the pen it sits in come from ART.pigpen, so a letter the film shows and a letter the lesson makes cannot disagree. The scenes file checks the spoken claims (cat is fdw, y shifted 3 is b, kl says hi) against those rules as the page loads.
title: Caesar and Pigpen
subtitle: Grade 4 Computing
objectives: Know how to write and decode messages using the Caesar Cipher and the Pigpen Cipher.
Identify where and why encryption is used in digital systems.

beats.say: Julius Caesar wanted to send orders that nobody else could read.
So he hid them in a cipher: a rule that turns a message into secret code.

at.rule: a rule that turns a message into secret code

beats.say: Caesar moved every letter the same number of places along the alphabet.
That number is the key. With a shift of three, a becomes d.
So cat becomes f d w. Each letter has moved three places along.
At the end of the alphabet you wrap round to the start. y shifted three is b.
To read it, shift back by the same number. f d w says cat again.
Pigpen does not shift letters. It swaps each one for a shape.
Draw a grid like noughts and crosses. Put a to i in its nine pens.

at.grid: a grid like noughts and crosses

beats.say: A letter's symbol is the shape of the lines round its pen.
a is in the top-left pen, so a is a corner, open at the top and left.
e sits in the middle pen, with lines all round, so e is a closed box.
A second grid holds j to r, each pen with a dot. Two X shapes hold s to z.
Write cat in Pigpen and you get three shapes. Read them back: cat.
A cipher is only as secret as its key. Whoever holds the key reads it.

at.secret: only as secret as its key

beats.say: Caesar had to tell his generals the shift in advance.
If a messenger carrying the key was caught, every message was open.
A Caesar cipher has only twenty-five shifts to try.
Try them one by one until words appear. It is a good puzzle and a weak lock.
Your browser and your messages use the very same idea.
Scramble the message with a key. Unscramble it with the key.
The difference is the key. Today's keys are enormously long.
Trying every one would take longer than the age of the universe.
That is why your password and your card number are safe on the way.
Every cipher makes the same journey, and each stage has a name.
You start with plain text: the message anybody could read.
You encrypt it with the key, and out comes ciphertext.

at.encrypt: You encrypt it with the key

beats.say: It travels. At the other end the key decrypts it.
The plain text is back. Caesar and Pigpen both make that trip.
Caesar shifts every letter along the alphabet by the key.
Pigpen gives every letter the shape of the pen it sits in.
The key is the secret, and twenty-five shifts is a weak secret.
Plain text in, ciphertext out, and the key brings it back.
